[Molly Scott Cato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Scott_Cato "Molly Scott Cato")[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-48) and by _[The Ecologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ecologist "The Ecologist")_ magazine.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-49)

In an interview with the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial\_Times "Financial Times")_, in August 2015, Corbyn pledged to renationalise the [Big Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Six_energy_suppliers "Big Six energy suppliers") energy companies[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-50) and to also bring the [National Grid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Grid_(Great_Britain) "National Grid (Great Britain)") into the public sector.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-51) In response to the announcement, financial analysts at [Jefferies Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferies_Group "Jefferies Group") LLC published a report estimating that the cost of such policies could reach £185 billion.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-52) On the same day that his energy policies were announced, Corbyn also told [Greenpeace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenpeace "Greenpeace")'s _Energy Desk_ website that he would consider re-opening the [South Wales Coalfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Wales_Coalfield "South Wales Coalfield"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-53) a suggestion that drew some criticism from some environmentalists and from [Yvette Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Cooper "Yvette Cooper"), one of Corbyn's opponents for the leadership, who accused him of making "false promises".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-54)

### Health

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Health")]

Corbyn has long campaigned against the "creeping privatisation" of [NHS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service_(England) "National Health Service (England)") services.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-55) For example, he has been critical of the [Blair government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Tony_Blair "Premiership of Tony Blair")'s use of [private finance initiatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_finance_initiative "Private finance initiative") as a source of public sector procurement, particularly its involvement in the construction of NHS hospitals. He has suggested that the [Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HM_Treasury "HM Treasury") should [bail out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailout "Bailout") hospitals struggling to pay off debt resulting from PFI deals.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-56) Corbyn has also released a policy document on addressing the lack of funding for care and the stigma and discrimination facing those that experience [mental health problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mental_disorders_in_the_DSM-IV_and_DSM-IV-TR "List of mental disorders in the DSM-IV and DSM-IV-TR").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-57)

### Immigration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Immigration")]

Corbyn has spoken of the socio-economic and cultural benefits of [immigration to the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_to_the_United_Kingdom "Immigration to the United Kingdom"), particularly of [multiculturalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiculturalism "Multiculturalism") and the high number of immigrant workers employed by the [National Health Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service_(England) "National Health Service (England)"). He also condemned the Labour Party's [2015 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election") manifesto pledge to reduce levels of immigration as "appalling".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-58) Corbyn has accused [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron") of using "incendiary language" when he accused a "swarm" of people as the cause of the [Calais migrant crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais_migrant_crisis "Calais migrant crisis")[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-59) and also described the [Home Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Office "Home Office")'s response to the [refugees of the Syrian civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugees_of_the_Syrian_civil_war "Refugees of the Syrian civil war") as "heartless and powerless", during the Sky News debate in September 2015.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-60)

### Welfare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Welfare")]

At the Second Reading of the [Welfare Reform and Work Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_Reform_and_Work_Bill "Welfare Reform and Work Bill") in July 2015, Corbyn joined 47 other Labour MPs to oppose the bill, describing it as "rotten and indefensible", whilst the other three candidates abstained.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-61) In August 2015, he called on [Iain Duncan Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Duncan_Smith "Iain Duncan Smith") to resign as [Secretary of State for Work and Pensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Work_and_Pensions "Secretary of State for Work and Pensions") after it emerged that thousands of disabled people had died after being found fit to work by [Work Capability Assessments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_Capability_Assessment "Work Capability Assessment") between 2011 and 2014.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-62) At the [Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian") Live leadership hustings, Corbyn condemned the reforms that had taken place since 2010, pledged that he would defend the [welfare state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state_in_the_United_Kingdom "Welfare state in the United Kingdom") as leader and insisted that politicians should show "a heart" when addressing issues of poverty and homelessness[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-63)

### Unionism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Unionism")]

In August 2015, when asked by Glasgow's _[Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Herald\_(Glasgow) "The Herald (Glasgow)")_ newspaper if he would describe himself as a [British unionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_unionist "British unionist"), Corbyn replied "No, I would describe myself as a socialist. I would prefer the UK to stay together, yes, but I recognise the right of people to take the decision on their own autonomy and independence". He also criticised the decision by [Scottish Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Labour "Scottish Labour") to work with Conservatives in the [Better Together](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_Together_(campaign) "Better Together (campaign)") campaign, and said that he had not actively participated in the referendum campaign. Corbyn also stated his belief that economic inequality exists across the UK, and that Labour should unite people on the basis of a "radical economic strategy".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-64)

On the subject of forming alliances with the [SNP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") after the 2020 general election Corbyn was the only leadership candidate who confirmed he would be open to working with the party, saying to [Aaron Bastani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Bastani "Aaron Bastani") of [Novara Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novara_Media "Novara Media") that "If there isn't a Labour majority but a minority and we've got to work with other parties – probably on the basis of a day-to-day arrangement or ... a supply arrangement then do that"[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-65)

## Foreign policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Foreign policy")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Jeremy_Corbyn%2C_Tolpuddle_2015.JPG/250px-Jeremy_Corbyn%2C_Tolpuddle_2015.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeremy_Corbyn,_Tolpuddle_2015.JPG)

Corbyn speaking at the [Tolpuddle Martyrs' Festival and Rally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolpuddle_Martyrs'_Festival_and_Rally "Tolpuddle Martyrs' Festival and Rally") in 2015

### Defence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Defence")]

Corbyn also stated his opposition to meeting the [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") requirement of 2% of GDP spending on defence, arguing at the _[Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mirror "Daily Mirror")_ hustings event, in August 2015, that NATO "should have been wound up in 1990" when the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") ended.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-66) However this position was criticised by [Ben Judah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Judah "Ben Judah") in _[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Independent "The Independent")_,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-IND150820-67) and by fellow candidate [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"), who said he would resign from a Corbyn shadow cabinet over such a policy.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-68)

On the 70th Anniversary of the [Hiroshima bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki"), Corbyn released a policy document detailing his opposition to the renewal of the [Trident missile system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trident_(UK_nuclear_programme) "Trident (UK nuclear programme)"), citing his support for unilateral [nuclear disarmament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament "Nuclear disarmament"). Corbyn suggested that the 11,000 jobs supported by [Trident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trident_(UK_nuclear_programme) "Trident (UK nuclear programme)") could be replaced by "socially productive" jobs in renewable energy, railways and housing.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-guardian-20150806-70)

In September 2015, it was reported that Corbyn had been advised, by members of his campaign team, to put his controversial positions on NATO and the renewal of Trident "on the back-burner" in order to unify the party and prevent high-profile, moderate shadow ministers, such as Burnham and [Chuka Umunna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuka_Umunna "Chuka Umunna"), from resigning.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-71)

### European Union

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: European Union")]

In June 2015, following a series of unsuccessful talks between the [Syriza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syriza "Syriza")-led [government of Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Cabinet_of_Alexis_Tsipras "First Cabinet of Alexis Tsipras") and [its creditors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troika_(European_group) "Troika (European group)") to agree the terms of a [third bailout deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Economic_Adjustment_Programme_for_Greece "Third Economic Adjustment Programme for Greece"), Corbyn accused the latter of being "determined to navigate [Greece] against the rocks, for daring to [vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_2015_Greek_parliamentary_election "January 2015 Greek parliamentary election") for a better future".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-72) At a party hustings in [Warrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington "Warrington"), in July 2015, Corbyn speculated that, should [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron") be unable to protect workers' rights and environmental protection laws in his negotiations with [European leaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Council "European Council"), he would be prepared to support a 'No' vote in the proposed referendum on EU membership.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-73) His words were met with criticism from the other leadership candidates, notably [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall"), who responded by saying that the party ought to be "unashamedly pro-EU".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-74)

In August 2015, [Nigel Farage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Farage "Nigel Farage"), Leader of the [UK Independence Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Independence_Party "UK Independence Party"), wrote in _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_, inviting Corbyn to join him to campaign in favour of [withdrawing from the EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_from_the_European_Union "Withdrawal from the European Union").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-75) Corbyn, however, re-affirmed his [pro-Europeanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-Europeanism "Pro-Europeanism") and support for the UK remaining a member of the European Union.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-76)

### West Asia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: West Asia")]

Corbyn is a prominent member of [Stop the War Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop_the_War_Coalition "Stop the War Coalition") and the [Palestine Solidarity Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine_Solidarity_Campaign "Palestine Solidarity Campaign").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Palestine-77) He holds an '[anti-interventionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-interventionist "Anti-interventionist")' position on foreign affairs, opposing [current British action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_military_intervention_against_ISIL "International military intervention against ISIL") against [Daesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daesh "Daesh") in the [Syrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war"), [Libyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_civil_war_(2014%E2%80%932020) "Libyan civil war (2014–2020)") and [Iraqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Iraq_(2013%E2%80%932017) "War in Iraq (2013–2017)") conflicts.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-78) He has also campaigned for the [recognition of Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recognition_of_Palestine "Recognition of Palestine") and been a long-standing [critic of Israel and the Israeli government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criticism_of_the_Israeli_government "Criticism of the Israeli government"). At a public meeting organised by _[The Jewish Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jewish\_Chronicle "The Jewish Chronicle")_ in July 2015, Corbyn called for an [arms embargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_embargo "Arms embargo") on Israel.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-79) In an interview with _The Daily Telegraph_ in September 2015, the Deputy Foreign Minister of the [Palestinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine "Palestine") territory of [Gaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip"), [Ghazi Hamad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghazi_Hamad "Ghazi Hamad"), supported Corbyn for his "sympathetic" stance on the [Israeli–Palestinian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-80) However, Corbyn's views on the conflict have also been criticised by _The Jewish Chronicle_[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-81) and [Joan Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Ryan_(politician) "Joan Ryan (politician)"), the Chairman of [Labour Friends of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Friends_of_Israel "Labour Friends of Israel").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-82)

In August 2015, Corbyn stated that if he became Labour leader, he would issue a public apology, on behalf of the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)"), for its role in the [2003 American-led invasion of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_American_invasion_of_Iraq "2003 American invasion of Iraq") by Britain, and for the resulting [murder of hundreds of thousands of Iraqi civilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casualties_of_the_Iraq_War#Iraqi_civilian_casualties "Casualties of the Iraq War") and some [179 British soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_British_casualties_during_the_Iraq_War "List of British casualties during the Iraq War").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-83) Corbyn also suggested that, should the [Chilcot Inquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilcot_Inquiry "Chilcot Inquiry") find former [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom")[Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair") guilty of [war crimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_crime "War crime"), he should stand [trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_crimes_trial "War crimes trial").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-84)

In an appearance on _[Question Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Question\_Time\_(TV\_programme) "Question Time (TV programme)")_ in July 2015, Corbyn suggested that the growth of the [Daesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daesh "Daesh") may have been aided by Britain's arms sales to authoritarian [Gulf states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_states_of_the_Persian_Gulf "Arab states of the Persian Gulf") such as [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar") and [Bahrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahrain "Bahrain").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-85)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Controversies")]

### Accusations of judeophobia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Accusations of judeophobia")]

In August 2015, several publications queried Corbyn's connection with people and organisations accused of [judeophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judeophobia "Judeophobia") such as [Raed Salah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raed_Salah "Raed Salah") and Paul Eisen of Deir Yassin Remembered.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-graun-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-DYR-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Vale-88) Corbyn rejoined that when he met Salah, he was unaware that he had been convicted of racial incitement,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-89) and that he had not made judeophobic comments during their conversation about Israel.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Vale-88) He also confirmed that he had attended DYR events and made limited cash donations but has "no contact now whatsoever" with the DYR director, previously accused of being a Holocaust denier.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-PSC-90) Corbyn described Holocaust denial as "obviously vile"[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-91) and his office released a statement to say he is "proud to represent a multicultural constituency of people from all over the world and to speak at every opportunity of understanding between Christian, Hindu, Jewish, Muslim and other faiths."[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-92)

_[The Jewish Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jewish\_Chronicle "The Jewish Chronicle")_ described Corbyn's response as unsatisfactory[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-94) but leading [Jewish critics of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Anti-Zionism "Jewish Anti-Zionism") defended Corbyn a week later in an open letter to the newspaper.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-JCAZ-95) Fellow MP [Diane Abbott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott "Diane Abbott") also said that "there will always be people who are less than savoury in liberation movements" and suggested that Corbyn is being [smeared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smear_campaign "Smear campaign") by people trying to make him guilty by association: "the British establishment is frozen with fear about the prospect of his victory".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-96)

### Women-only railway carriages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Women-only railway carriages")]

Corbyn raised the possibility in August 2015 of introducing [women-only carriages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women-only_carriage "Women-only carriage") on public transport, as well as a 24-hour hotline for women to report cases of harassment. He said that although his aim was to "make public transport safer for everyone from the train platform, to the bus stop to the mode of transport itself", he would consult women on whether such carriages would be welcome, after the idea was suggested to him.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-GuardTransport-97)

His proposal was condemned by all three rival Leadership candidates, Yvette Cooper, Andy Burnham and Liz Kendall, with Cooper stating that Corbyn's plan was "turning the clock back instead of tackling the problem",[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-98) while Conservative Women's Minister [Nicky Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicky_Morgan "Nicky Morgan") said she was "uncomfortable with the idea", which sounded like "segregation".[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-99)

## Opinion polling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Opinion polling")]

See also: [2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK) §Opinion polling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#Opinion_polling "2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)")

On 21 July 2015, a [YouGov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouGov "YouGov") poll for _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_, sampling the voting intentions of current Labour Party members, projected Corbyn to win the leadership election, with 43% of first preferences and 53% of the final redistributed total.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-100) The surge in popularity was reported to have greatly surprised even Corbyn himself.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-101) On 11 August, _The Times_ published the results of its second YouGov poll, indicating that Corbyn was on course for a "decisive victory"; it claimed that support for Corbyn had increased further to 57% and that he would therefore win on first preferences.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-102)_[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ reported a Survation poll showing that, after being shown a short video of all four candidates, more voters from both the wider electorate and previous Labour, [Liberal Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") and [UK Independence Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Independence_Party "UK Independence Party") (UKIP) voters indicated a preference for Corbyn.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-103)

However, on 15 August, _[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Independent "The Independent") on Sunday_ reported a [ComRes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ComRes "ComRes") poll it had commissioned of the general public, revealing that if Corbyn were to become Labour Leader, voters believed it would reduce Labour's chances of winning the next election, whilst the election of [David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband"), who was defeated by his brother in 2010, would stand the best chance of Labour winning the next election.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-104)

## Momentum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Momentum")]

Main article: [Momentum (organisation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum_(organisation) "Momentum (organisation)")

Corbyn was announced to have been elected [Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)"), at a conference held in central London, with over 59% of first-preference votes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Result-9) Following this result, a new group called _Momentum_ was formed. Momentum describes itself as a [grassroots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassroots "Grassroots") political [advocacy group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advocacy_group "Advocacy group") which grew out of the Jeremy Corbyn for Labour Leader campaign[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-BBC_News:_Momentum-105) which describes itself as "a network of people and organisations that will continue the energy and enthusiasm of Jeremy's campaign".[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-106) The idea was denounced by Labour critics of the leader as part of an attempt to mobilise factionally, leading to the deselection of moderate MPs and councillors "who are not judged [politically correct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politically_correct "Politically correct") by the veteran [Bennite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennite "Bennite") organisers behind Momentum".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-107)As of October 2015[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign&action=edit) Momentum had about 60,000 supporters, charges no membership fee, organises mostly through social media and has around 50 local groups across the UK.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-BBC_News:_Momentum-105)

Labour MP and former shadow minister [Emma Reynolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Reynolds "Emma Reynolds") describes Momentum as "a parallel organisation to the Labour Party" (something which the organisation denies[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Guardian:_Momentum-108)) and likened them to the [Militant tendency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Militant_tendency "Militant tendency").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-BBC_News:_Momentum-105) Some [hard left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_left "Hard left") groups have attempted to affiliate themselves with the organisation, thus causing concern among the [soft left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_left "Soft left") of the Labour Party.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Guardian:_Momentum-108) Others on the [far left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_left "Far left") have criticised the group strongly.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-109)

The **2015 Labour Party leadership election** was triggered by the resignation of [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") as [Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") on 8 May 2015, following the party's defeat at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"). [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman"), the [Deputy Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)"), became Acting Leader but announced that she would stand down following the leadership election.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-1) It was won by [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") in the first round. In the [2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election"), which was run simultaneously, [Tom Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Watson,_Baron_Watson_of_Wyre_Forest "Tom Watson, Baron Watson of Wyre Forest") was elected to succeed Harman as deputy leader.

Four candidates were successfully nominated to stand in the election: [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"), [Yvette Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Cooper "Yvette Cooper"), Jeremy Corbyn, and [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall"). The voting process began on Friday 14 August 2015 and closed on Thursday 10 September 2015, and the results were announced on Saturday 12 September 2015. Voting was by [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") members and registered and affiliated supporters, using the [alternative vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_vote "Alternative vote") system.

Support for Corbyn, who entered the race as a [dark horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_horse "Dark horse") candidate,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-2) and the release of opinion polls which showed him leading the race, led to high-profile interventions by a number of prominent Labour figures including [Gordon Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Brown "Gordon Brown"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-3)[Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-4)[Jack Straw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Straw "Jack Straw"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-5)[David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-6) and [Alastair Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alastair_Campbell "Alastair Campbell"), among others,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-7) many of whom argued that Corbyn's election as leader would leave the party unelectable.

Despite these interventions, Corbyn was elected in the first round receiving 59.5% of the votes, winning in all three sections of the ballot. Less than a year later, a leadership challenge saw another [leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), where Corbyn again won, with an increased share of the vote. In July 2026, Burnham succeeded [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer") as Labour leader.

## Procedure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Procedure")]

The leadership election, triggered by [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband")'s resignation, took place under the reformed rules adopted from the proposals of the February 2014 Collins Report, which was led by [Ray Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Collins,_Baron_Collins_of_Highbury "Ray Collins, Baron Collins of Highbury"), and was itself partly the result of calls for inquiry and reform relating to the [2013 Falkirk Selection Scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Labour_Party_Falkirk_candidate_selection "2013 Labour Party Falkirk candidate selection").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-8) The plan entailed a shorter election than the one that took place in [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2010 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), with a new leader being in place before [Labour's party conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_Conference "Labour Party Conference") in September 2015.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-9)

The review changed the way in which Labour elects leaders. Under the former system, a three-way [electoral college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_college "Electoral college") chose the leader, with one-third weight given to the votes of the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party") (i.e., Labour members of the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") and Labour [members of the European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Members_of_the_European_Parliament "Members of the European Parliament")), one-third to individual Labour Party members, and one third to the trade union and [affiliated societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_society_(Labour_Party) "Socialist society (Labour Party)") sections. Following the Collins review, the electoral college was replaced by a pure "[one member, one vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_member,_one_vote "One member, one vote")" (OMOV) system. Candidates are elected by members and registered and affiliated supporters, who all receive a maximum of one vote and all votes are weighted equally.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-independent-20140228-10) This meant that, for example, members of Labour-affiliated trade unions needed to register as Labour supporters to vote.

To stand, candidates now needed to be nominated by at least 15% of the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party") (PLP), i.e. 35 [MPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)"), at that time. The vote, as in previous elections, was held under the [alternative vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_vote "Alternative vote") (instant-runoff) system. The [deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election") was held under the same rules.

The election itself was overseen by [Electoral Reform Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Reform_Services "Electoral Reform Services").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-11)

In late August, the Labour Party reported that about 552,000 members and supporters were eligible to vote; about 292,000 full members, 148,000 affiliated supporters (members of trade unions and [socialist societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_societies "Socialist societies") who opted to affiliate), plus 112,000 registered supporters.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-independent-20150910-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-mirror-20150825-13)

### Timetable

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Timetable")]

A meeting of Labour's [National Executive Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Executive_Committee_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "National Executive Committee of the Labour Party (UK)") took place on 13 May 2015 to set a timetable and procedure for the two elections.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-BBCTimetable-14)

*   _Tuesday 9 June 2015_ – Nominations open
*   _Monday 15 June 2015 (12:00)_ – Nominations for the Leader close
*   _Wednesday 17 June 2015 (12:00)_ – Nominations for the [Deputy Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election") close
*   _Wednesday 17 June 2015 (12:00)_ – [Hustings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husting "Husting") period opens
*   _Friday 31 July 2015 (12:00)_ – Supporting nominations close
*   _Wednesday 12 August 2015 (15:00)_ – Last date to join as member, affiliated support or registered supporter and be able to vote[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-15)
*   _Friday 14 August 2015_ – Ballot papers are sent out
*   _Thursday 10 September 2015 (12:00)_ – Ballot closes
*   _Saturday 12 September 2015_ – [Special Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_Conference "Labour Party Conference") to announce the results

The deadline on 12 August 2015 to join as a member or supporter was extended by 3 hours due to heavy demand making the party website difficult to use.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-telegraph-20150812-16)

## Media reaction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Media reaction")]

### Burnham

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Burnham")]

Burnham was praised for having both "a radical left-wing vision" and being credible enough "to unite the party and win back power",[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-55) as well as for being someone who "actually listens to party members and the public".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-56)

Burnham attracted press criticism for claiming £17,000 a year from the taxpayer to rent a London flat, despite owning another within walking distance of the House of Commons. A spokesman for Burnham said that renting out the original flat was necessary to "cover his costs" as parliamentary rule changes meant he was no longer able to claim for mortgage interest expenses.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-57) Burnham was criticised for saying that Labour should have a woman leader "when the time is right", with the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_ saying that he had "tripped over his mouth again".

### Cooper

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Cooper")]

Cooper was praised by the _[Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huffington\_Post "Huffington Post")_ for her hard work in local constituencies during the leadership contest[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-huffingtonpost.co.uk-58) and for her preparation for the Local Government Association hustings.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-59)

She has been criticised both for thanking [David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband") for putting her as his second choice (after [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall"))[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-60) and for her "broken, downbeat delivery".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-61)

### Corbyn

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Corbyn")]

Corbyn's leadership bid was the subject of fierce discussion within the media. [Janan Ganesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janan_Ganesh "Janan Ganesh") in the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial\_Times "Financial Times")_ argued that the election of Corbyn "spells disaster" for the Labour Party.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-62)[Owen Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Jones "Owen Jones") argued in _The Guardian_ that the reason Corbyn was so popular was because he "offers a coherent, inspiring and, crucially, a hopeful vision" addressing social injustice and economic inequality, comparing the surge of support for Corbyn to the popularity of both UKIP in England and the [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") (SNP) in Scotland.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-63)

### Kendall

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Kendall")]

In June 2015, Kendall's leadership bid received praise from _[The Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sun\_(United\_Kingdom) "The Sun (United Kingdom)")_, who said that she is the "only prayer they [the Labour Party] have". _The Sun_ also praised her for saying 'the country comes first' in response to [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") who said 'the [Labour] Party always comes first' in the _[Newsnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsnight "Newsnight")_ Labour leadership hustings.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-64)[Commentators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pundit "Pundit") from across the political spectrum have said that Kendall is the leadership candidate that the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") "fear the most".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-67)

However, the Huffington Post criticised her, saying "[Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall") just doesn't seem to have it, she seems to be always on the verge of tripping over her own words, as if she is perpetually being caught off guard."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-huffingtonpost.co.uk-58)

One of the most notable features of the election was the large increase in Labour Party membership, and the registration of significant numbers of the new affiliated and registered classes of voting supporters, during the period of the campaign.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc-20150812-68) Concern was expressed that the new rules were unfairly benefiting Corbyn,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc-20150810-69) and there might be a legal challenge,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-spectator-20150825-70) but in the event the result was so decisive these concerns were not pursued after the election.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-independent-20150912-71)

In June 2015, the Conservative-identifying political commentator [Toby Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Young "Toby Young") wrote in the _Telegraph_ encouraging Conservatives to join Labour to vote for [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn"),[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-72) his reason being "to consign Labour to electoral oblivion". This trended on Twitter as #ToriesforCorbyn and the attempt, as well as Labour's response, were subject to criticism.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-73) Two days later the [Communist Party of Great Britain (Provisional Central Committee)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Great_Britain_(Provisional_Central_Committee) "Communist Party of Great Britain (Provisional Central Committee)") wrote also in support of Corbyn.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-74) Following this, Labour MP [John Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mann,_Baron_Mann "John Mann, Baron Mann") called for the election to be halted.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-75) Acting leader of the party [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman") responded by calling on constituency parties to check new members, but stated that Labour has "a robust system to prevent fraudulent or malicious applications." Labour MP [Fabian Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_Hamilton "Fabian Hamilton") stated there was "no evidence" that groups were trying to infiltrate the election.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-76) Leadership candidates [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") and [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall") also responded by saying there was no evidence of infiltration, and while not dismissing the claims, Corbyn stated he only wanted "genuine Labour supporters" to vote for him.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-78)

### Rejected voters

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Rejected voters")]

It emerged in early August 2015 that 260 former candidates from the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales "Green Party of England and Wales"), [Left Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_Unity_(UK) "Left Unity (UK)") and the [Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_Unionist_and_Socialist_Coalition "Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition") had attempted to become registered supporters but would now be blocked from voting.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-79) Shortly before this it was revealed that Conservative MP and former junior minister [Tim Loughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Loughton "Tim Loughton") had been caught applying to become a registered Labour supporter, subsequently claiming that his intention was to "blow the gaff on what a complete farce the whole thing is".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-80) Veteran Labour MP [Barry Sheerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Sheerman "Barry Sheerman") also joined calls for the election to be "paused" over the fears of infiltration by other parties.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc-20150810-69) The Labour Party told representatives of the four candidates at a meeting on 11 August that 1,200 members and supporters of other parties had been excluded and a further 800 were under investigation.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-81) Harriet Harman at the time admitted that as many as 100,000 people may be blocked from voting.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-82)

The number of those rejected would eventually reach 56,000,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-83) around 9.1% of the 610,753 considered eligible to vote at the start of the contest.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-84) According to the party, 45,000 of those were rejected for not being on the [electoral register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_registration_in_the_United_Kingdom "Electoral registration in the United Kingdom").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-85)

Labour also confirmed that it would cancel supporters' votes after they had been cast if it was found that they were members of other parties.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-86) A number of high-profile individuals were blocked from voting, including [Marcus Chown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Chown "Marcus Chown"),[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-scriptonitedaily.com-87)[Jeremy Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Hardy "Jeremy Hardy"), [Douglas Henshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Henshall "Douglas Henshall"),[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-auto-88)[Ken Loach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Loach "Ken Loach"),[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-scriptonitedaily.com-87)[Francesca Martinez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesca_Martinez "Francesca Martinez"),[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-auto-88)[Mark Serwotka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Serwotka "Mark Serwotka"),[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-89)[Pete Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Sinclair_(writer) "Pete Sinclair (writer)"),[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-90)[Mark Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Steel "Mark Steel"),[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-91)[Luke Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_Wright_(poet) "Luke Wright (poet)")[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-92) and [Toby Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Young "Toby Young").

[Andrew MacKinlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_MacKinlay "Andrew MacKinlay"), a former Labour MP, further alleged that Labour was attempting to rig its own leadership election against Corbyn;[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-93) a view shared by comedian [Jeremy Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Hardy "Jeremy Hardy").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-94) Such allegations became known to the media – and particularly Corbyn supporters – as the "Labour [Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purge "Purge")", with #LabourPurge trending on Twitter.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-96) Claims of such a "purge" of Corbyn supporters were rejected by Harman who insisted that the exclusion processes were impartial to candidates.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-spectator-20150825-70) Scottish newspaper _[The National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_National\_(Scotland) "The National (Scotland)")_ printed a page-long satirical cartoon speculating further vote-rigging by Labour's leadership.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-97)

### Missing ballots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Missing ballots")]

With less than 24 hours to go before the voting deadline, the party closed their telephone helpline. The move came during widespread complaints from "thousands" of voters who were missing emailed or physical ballot papers.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-98)_The Guardian_ reported that one of their sources in the leadership camps stated that "the party has basically decided to stop taking calls and if you don't have a vote, you're now basically not getting one."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-99) The party refused to confirm how many ballot papers had actually been sent.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-100)[Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") publicly criticised the number of missing ballots and the closure of the phone line.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-101)

Labour MP [David Lammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lammy "David Lammy") called for a full inquiry into the missing ballot papers.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-102) Of the 200 people his team phone called in London on the eve of the deadline, one in five were missing their ballots.

## Political reaction to the result

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Political reaction to the result")]

### Domestic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Domestic")]

Labour Party
[Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband"), former [party leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)"), offered his support to Corbyn and urged other Labour MPs to do so, though he ruled himself out of taking on a position in [Corbyn's shadow cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corbyn's_shadow_cabinet "Corbyn's shadow cabinet"), to focus on representing his constituency.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-138)[Kezia Dugdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kezia_Dugdale "Kezia Dugdale"), then leader of [Scottish Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Labour "Scottish Labour"), declared that "politics has changed" and people desired a "radical change", with Corbyn's election to the leadership showing that Labour had "listened to that call".[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-ScotReact-139)[Carwyn Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carwyn_Jones "Carwyn Jones"), then leader of [Welsh Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Labour "Welsh Labour") and [First Minister of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Minister_of_Wales "First Minister of Wales"), congratulated Corbyn and urged the party to embrace the fact that the campaign had "energised a huge number of people who were previously disengaged from party politics" and unite around their new leader.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-140)

Corbyn's rivals for the leadership each reacted to the result. [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") said that [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") was a politician with "very deep beliefs, very strong principles" which voters would embrace.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-141) Burnham later replaced [Yvette Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Cooper "Yvette Cooper") as [Shadow Home Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Home_Secretary "Shadow Home Secretary") after she announced that she would not serve on a Labour frontbench led by Corbyn and that she would instead focus on playing a role in the [upcoming EU membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-142) Following the close of voting, [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall") made a speech reflecting on her campaign stating that, after the [New Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Labour "New Labour") government, there was never any debate in relation to the direction the party should go, and it had created a split "between the party and the country".[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-143) All three of Corbyn's opponents in the leadership election stated they would support Corbyn, that the result should be accepted and the party should focus on attacking the Conservative government.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-144)

During the announcement of Corbyn's victory, [Jamie Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_Reed "Jamie Reed") resigned as a Shadow Health Minister, citing his difference in opinion, with the new leader, over the replacement of the [Trident missile system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trident_(UK_nuclear_programme) "Trident (UK nuclear programme)"). The **2015 Labour Party leadership election** was triggered by the resignation of [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") as [Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") on 8 May 2015, following the party's defeat at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"). [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman"), the [Deputy Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)"), became Acting Leader but announced that she would stand down following the leadership election.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-1) It was won by [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") in the first round. In the [2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election"), which was run simultaneously, [Tom Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Watson,_Baron_Watson_of_Wyre_Forest "Tom Watson, Baron Watson of Wyre Forest") was elected to succeed Harman as deputy leader.

Four candidates were successfully nominated to stand in the election: [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"), [Yvette Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Cooper "Yvette Cooper"), Jeremy Corbyn, and [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall"). The voting process began on Friday 14 August 2015 and closed on Thursday 10 September 2015, and the results were announced on Saturday 12 September 2015. Voting was by [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") members and registered and affiliated supporters, using the [alternative vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_vote "Alternative vote") system.

Support for Corbyn, who entered the race as a [dark horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_horse "Dark horse") candidate,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-2) and the release of opinion polls which showed him leading the race, led to high-profile interventions by a number of prominent Labour figures including [Gordon Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Brown "Gordon Brown"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-3)[Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-4)[Jack Straw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Straw "Jack Straw"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-5)[David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-6) and [Alastair Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alastair_Campbell "Alastair Campbell"), among others,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-7) many of whom argued that Corbyn's election as leader would leave the party unelectable.

Despite these interventions, Corbyn was elected in the first round receiving 59.5% of the votes, winning in all three sections of the ballot. Less than a year later, a leadership challenge saw another [leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), where Corbyn again won, with an increased share of the vote. In July 2026, Burnham succeeded [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer") as Labour leader.

## Procedure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Procedure")]

The leadership election, triggered by [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband")'s resignation, took place under the reformed rules adopted from the proposals of the February 2014 Collins Report, which was led by [Ray Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Collins,_Baron_Collins_of_Highbury "Ray Collins, Baron Collins of Highbury"), and was itself partly the result of calls for inquiry and reform relating to the [2013 Falkirk Selection Scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Labour_Party_Falkirk_candidate_selection "2013 Labour Party Falkirk candidate selection").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-8) The plan entailed a shorter election than the one that took place in [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2010 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), with a new leader being in place before [Labour's party conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_Conference "Labour Party Conference") in September 2015.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-9)

The review changed the way in which Labour elects leaders. Under the former system, a three-way [electoral college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_college "Electoral college") chose the leader, with one-third weight given to the votes of the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party") (i.e., Labour members of the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") and Labour [members of the European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Members_of_the_European_Parliament "Members of the European Parliament")), one-third to individual Labour Party members, and one third to the trade union and [affiliated societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_society_(Labour_Party) "Socialist society (Labour Party)") sections. Following the Collins review, the electoral college was replaced by a pure "[one member, one vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_member,_one_vote "One member, one vote")" (OMOV) system. Candidates are elected by members and registered and affiliated supporters, who all receive a maximum of one vote and all votes are weighted equally.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-independent-20140228-10) This meant that, for example, members of Labour-affiliated trade unions needed to register as Labour supporters to vote.

To stand, candidates now needed to be nominated by at least 15% of the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party") (PLP), i.e. 35 [MPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)"), at that time. The vote, as in previous elections, was held under the [alternative vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_vote "Alternative vote") (instant-runoff) system. The [deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election") was held under the same rules.

The election itself was overseen by [Electoral Reform Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Reform_Services "Electoral Reform Services").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-11)

In late August, the Labour Party reported that about 552,000 members and supporters were eligible to vote; about 292,000 full members, 148,000 affiliated supporters (members of trade unions and [socialist societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_societies "Socialist societies") who opted to affiliate), plus 112,000 registered supporters.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-independent-20150910-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-mirror-20150825-13)

### Timetable

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Timetable")]

A meeting of Labour's [National Executive Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Executive_Committee_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "National Executive Committee of the Labour Party (UK)") took place on 13 May 2015 to set a timetable and procedure for the two elections.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-BBCTimetable-14)

*   _Tuesday 9 June 2015_ – Nominations open
*   _Monday 15 June 2015 (12:00)_ – Nominations for the Leader close
*   _Wednesday 17 June 2015 (12:00)_ – Nominations for the [Deputy Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election") close
*   _Wednesday 17 June 2015 (12:00)_ – [Hustings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husting "Husting") period opens
*   _Friday 31 July 2015 (12:00)_ – Supporting nominations close
*   _Wednesday 12 August 2015 (15:00)_ – Last date to join as member, affiliated support or registered supporter and be able to vote[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-15)
*   _Friday 14 August 2015_ – Ballot papers are sent out
*   _Thursday 10 September 2015 (12:00)_ – Ballot closes
*   _Saturday 12 September 2015_ – [Special Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_Conference "Labour Party Conference") to announce the results

The deadline on 12 August 2015 to join as a member or supporter was extended by 3 hours due to heavy demand making the party website difficult to use.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-telegraph-20150812-16)

## Media reaction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Media reaction")]

### Burnham

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Burnham")]

Burnham was praised for having both "a radical left-wing vision" and being credible enough "to unite the party and win back power",[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-55) as well as for being someone who "actually listens to party members and the public".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-56)

Burnham attracted press criticism for claiming £17,000 a year from the taxpayer to rent a London flat, despite owning another within walking distance of the House of Commons. A spokesman for Burnham said that renting out the original flat was necessary to "cover his costs" as parliamentary rule changes meant he was no longer able to claim for mortgage interest expenses.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-57) Burnham was criticised for saying that Labour should have a woman leader "when the time is right", with the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_ saying that he had "tripped over his mouth again".

### Cooper

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Cooper")]

Cooper was praised by the _[Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huffington\_Post "Huffington Post")_ for her hard work in local constituencies during the leadership contest[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-huffingtonpost.co.uk-58) and for her preparation for the Local Government Association hustings.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-59)

She has been criticised both for thanking [David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband") for putting her as his second choice (after [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall"))[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-60) and for her "broken, downbeat delivery".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-61)

### Corbyn

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Corbyn")]

Corbyn's leadership bid was the subject of fierce discussion within the media. [Janan Ganesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janan_Ganesh "Janan Ganesh") in the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial\_Times "Financial Times")_ argued that the election of Corbyn "spells disaster" for the Labour Party.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-62)[Owen Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Jones "Owen Jones") argued in _The Guardian_ that the reason Corbyn was so popular was because he "offers a coherent, inspiring and, crucially, a hopeful vision" addressing social injustice and economic inequality, comparing the surge of support for Corbyn to the popularity of both UKIP in England and the [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") (SNP) in Scotland.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-63)

### Kendall

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Kendall")]

In June 2015, Kendall's leadership bid received praise from _[The Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sun\_(United\_Kingdom) "The Sun (United Kingdom)")_, who said that she is the "only prayer they [the Labour Party] have". _The Sun_ also praised her for saying 'the country comes first' in response to [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") who said 'the [Labour] Party always comes first' in the _[Newsnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsnight "Newsnight")_ Labour leadership hustings.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-64)[Commentators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pundit "Pundit") from across the political spectrum have said that Kendall is the leadership candidate that the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") "fear the most".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-67)

However, the Huffington Post criticised her, saying "[Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall") just doesn't seem to have it, she seems to be always on the verge of tripping over her own words, as if she is perpetually being caught off guard."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-huffingtonpost.co.uk-58)
